review_candidates.title: VP, Services
review_candidates.description: Job Description ROLE PURPOSE The India Delivery Leader owns delivery execution across the P&C Services organization in India. The role is accountable for execution discipline, delivery quality, capacity, talent, operating consistency, and the effectiveness of the India delivery organization across all P&C portfolios. This is not an account P&L role and should not become another layer of program management. Portfolio Leaders own the business performance of their portfolios, including revenue, margin, growth, customer outcomes, and overall portfolio health. The India Delivery Leader ensures the delivery organization has the leadership, people, skills, methods, and operating discipline required to deliver those commitments. The role should create one P&C delivery organization rather than separate teams built around individual products, accounts, or leaders. CORE ACCOUNTABILITIES Delivery Execution Own execution discipline across P&C Services programs delivered from India. Ensure programs operate with clear plans, milestones, dependencies, risks, staffing models, and delivery controls. Hold India-based Delivery Managers accountable for execution against agreed customer commitments. Ensure delivery problems surface early, with clear ownership and recovery actions. Intervene when execution begins to drift, while keeping day-to-day program accountability with the Delivery Manager. Establish consistent expectations for planning, estimation, requirements management, build, testing, deployment, and production readiness. Quality Own delivery quality across the India organization. Drive P&C Services targets for measures such as leakage below agreed thresholds; rework below agreed thresholds; MTTR within agreed targets; aging issues within agreed targets; and release quality and production stability. Track quality trends across accounts rather than treating defects and rework as isolated project problems. Identify recurring causes of quality failure and drive corrective actions across the organization. Ensure teams address root causes instead of repeatedly absorbing rework. Capacity and workforce planning Own the India P&C delivery capacity plan. Maintain forward visibility into demand by portfolio, account, skill, location, and timing. Work with Portfolio Leaders to translate backlog, pipeline, and customer plans into staffing requirements. Balance resources across portfolios based on business priorities rather than allowing individual accounts to hold capacity unnecessarily. Identify capacity gaps early enough to hire, train, redeploy, or develop talent. Drive utilization while protecting delivery quality and the sustainability of the organization. Maintain a clear view of bench, open demand, critical skill shortages, and upcoming releases requiring concentrated capacity. Delivery leadership India-based Delivery Managers report to the India Delivery Leader. Assign Delivery Managers to portfolios and customer programs in partnership with Portfolio Leaders. Set clear standards for the Delivery Manager role. Delivery Managers should own day-to-day execution; integrated delivery planning; resource coordination; risk and dependency management; delivery metrics; quality and release readiness; India team leadership; and escalation of execution risks. Develop Delivery Managers who lead programs rather than operate as project coordinators. Address inconsistent leadership performance quickly. Create succession coverage for major programs and delivery leadership positions. Partnership with Portfolio Leaders The India Delivery Leader and Portfolio Leaders operate as peers with different accountabilities. Portfolio Leaders own portfolio P&L; revenue and margin; growth; customer executive relationships; commercial decisions; account strategy; and overall customer outcomes. The India Delivery Leader owns execution discipline; India delivery capability; Delivery Manager performance; resource deployment; quality discipline; skills and workforce readiness; and consistency of delivery methods. The two leaders jointly own staffing decisions, major delivery recovery plans, leadership coverage, and readiness for future demand. Where priorities conflict, decisions should reflect the overall P&C Services business rather than the interests of an individual account or delivery team. Operating discipline Create a common delivery operating model across P&C Services. Establish a consistent operating rhythm for program health, capacity, quality, staffing, and major delivery risks. Make delivery performance visible through a small set of meaningful measures. Reduce dependence on manually assembled status reporting. Ensure Delivery Managers maintain accurate plans and forecasts rather than rebuilding information immediately before leadership reviews. Identify programs requiring intervention based on data and delivery signals. Drive consistent use of program governance, estimation standards, entry and exit criteria, quality gates, and release controls. Ensure lessons from one implementation become operating improvements across other programs. AI and Automation Own adoption of P&C Services delivery methods and AI capabilities across the India organization. Move teams from isolated use of AI tools toward repeatable use within delivery workflows. Work with P&C Services leadership to measure the business effect of these capabilities. Expected outcomes include lower rework, shorter cycle times, improved quality, better planning accuracy, and reduced manual effort. Ensure teams use reusable assets and automation before creating new solutions from scratch. Identify areas where delivery practices should change because AI and automation have reduced the effort required for traditional activities. Do not measure success by the number of agents or tools deployed. Measure the effect on delivery performance. Talent and capability Own the capability plan for the India P&C Services organization. Maintain visibility into skills required across Policy, Billing, Claims, Digital, Data, migration, integrations, testing, and other P&C capabilities. Identify future skill requirements from the business pipeline rather than reacting after work is signed. Build stronger Delivery Managers and the next level of delivery leadership. Develop cross-account mobility so strong people are not locked permanently into individual customers. Work with functional leaders to develop specialists where deeper expertise is required. Create succession plans for critical roles. Address persistent performance issues. Ensure strong performers receive larger responsibilities rather than relying repeatedly on the same small group of leaders. Commercial awareness While the Portfolio Leader owns P&L, the India Delivery Leader must understand the commercial impact of delivery decisions. Ensure teams understand contracted scope, effort assumptions, staffing models, and delivery commitments. Challenge unplanned effort and uncontrolled scope expansion. Make additional effort visible to Portfolio Leaders before the organization absorbs the cost. Ensure staffing decisions consider both delivery need and account economics. Partner with Portfolio Leaders and Business Operations when delivery performance puts margin or revenue at risk. Delivery recovery Take an active leadership role when major programs move into distress. Establish the facts quickly. Determine whether the problem comes from scope, planning, capability, staffing, quality, product dependencies, customer dependencies, or leadership. Put a clear recovery structure in place. Assign accountable owners. Track recovery against measurable outcomes. Keep Portfolio Leaders informed of customer and commercial implications. Once the program stabilizes, address the organizational cause rather than simply closing the escalation. Enterprise leadership Operate as the leader of the India P&C delivery organization, not as the leader of one product or account group. Make resource and leadership decisions based on overall P&C priorities. Work across Product, Engineering, Cloud, Customer Success, Finance, and other Services groups where execution requires shared ownership. Bring problems to leadership with facts, options, and a recommendation. Challenge commitments the delivery organization cannot responsibly meet. Create an environment where teams raise risks early rather than protecting status reports. SUCCESS MEASURES Success should be measured through: Program delivery performance against committed milestones. Quality and production outcomes. Rework. Leakage. MTTR. Aging issues. Forecast accuracy for delivery staffing. Utilization. Bench and capacity management. Time required to fill critical roles. Delivery Manager performance. Reduction in late delivery escalations. Improvement in estimation and planning accuracy. Cross-portfolio resource mobility. Succession coverage for critical positions. Measured business benefit from APPEX, automation, and AI-enabled delivery practices. Experience And Background Senior leadership experience running large technology services or enterprise software delivery organizations in India. Strong experience with P&C insurance technology implementations or comparable enterprise software programs. Experience leading multiple customer programs and distributed delivery teams. Strong understanding of program delivery, implementation methods, quality management, workforce planning, and delivery economics. Experience leading Delivery Managers, Program Managers, engineering teams, testing organizations, business analysts, and other implementation disciplines. Experience managing organizations supporting US-based customers and senior customer executives. Strong working understanding of professional services economics, including utilization, staffing cost, margin drivers, scope management, and estimation. Experience building leadership capability and managing large-scale organizational change. Experience introducing automation, AI, reusable assets, or other delivery methods with measurable operational results. LEADERSHIP EXPECTATIONS The India Delivery Leader should be demanding about execution without becoming the person running every program. They should create accountability rather than become the escalation point for every decision. They should know the detail behind a troubled program while spending most of their time improving the system that produces delivery results. They should be comfortable challenging Portfolio Leaders when commitments exceed delivery capacity, and equally comfortable challenging India leaders when execution falls short of commitments already made. The strongest evidence of success will be an India delivery organization that performs consistently without depending on heroic intervention from senior leaders.
